plain_english: Maybe you're wondering what I mean by "busy men." I'm not just talking about lawyers who get chased out of courtrooms when court ends, or those you see either proudly surrounded by their own clients or rudely pushed around by strangers during formal visits. I don't just mean the ones who drag them away from home to wait around at their patron's door, or who use the praetor's auctions to make shameful profits that will eventually destroy them. Some people are busy even in their leisure time. At their country house or lying on their couch, completely alone, even when they've withdrawn from all society, they still keep worrying themselves sick. We shouldn't call this kind of life leisurely — their business is actually laziness.
original_excerpt: Perhaps you will ask me whom I mean by "busy men"? you need not think that I allude only to those who are hunted out of the courts of justice with dogs at the close of the proceedings, those whom you see either honourably jostled by a crowd of their own clients or contemptuously hustled in visits of ceremony by strangers, who call them away from home to hang about their patron's doors, or who make use of the praetor's sales by auction to acquire infamous gains which some day will prove their own ruin. Some men's leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men's society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men's life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Would you call a man idle who spends anxious hours arranging his collection of Corinthian bronze statues — valuable only because a few collectors have gone crazy for them? A man who spends most of his days among plates of rusty metal? Who sits in the gymnasium (how shameful that even our vices come from abroad) watching boys wrestle? Who sorts his chained slaves into matching pairs by age and skin color? Who keeps fashionable athletes on his payroll?
original_excerpt: Would you call a man idle who expends anxious finicking care in the arrangement of his Corinthian bronzes, valuable only through the mania of a few connoisseurs? and who passes the greater part of his days among plates of rusty metal? who sits in the palaestra (shame, that our very vices should be foreign) watching boys wrestling? who distributes his gangs of fettered slaves into pairs according to their age and colour? who keeps athletes of the latest fashion?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Do you really think those men are idle who spend hours at the barber? They sit there while last night's stubble gets plucked out by the roots. They hold meetings about every single hair. They arrange scattered locks just so, forcing back hair forward onto their foreheads. How furious they get if the barber slips up a little — as if he were cutting a real man! They work themselves into a rage if any of their precious mane gets trimmed wrong. If some part doesn't sit right. If all their curls don't lie in perfect rows. Which of them wouldn't rather see the government collapse than have his hair messed up? Which one doesn't care more about how his head looks than his actual health? Which one wouldn't choose decoration over honor?
original_excerpt: Why, do you call those men idle, who pass many hours at the barber's while the growth of the past night is being plucked out by the roots, holding councils over each several hair, while the scattered locks are arranged in order and those which fall back are forced forward on to the forehead? How angry they become if the shaver is a little careless, as though he were shearing a _man_! what a white heat they work themselves into if some of their mane is cut away, if some part of it is ill-arranged, if all their ringlets do not lie in regular order! who of them would not rather that the state were overthrown than that his hair should be ruffled? who does not care more for the appearance of his head than for his health? who would not prefer ornament to honour?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Do you think these men are idle — the ones who spend all their time fussing with their hair and mirrors? What about those who devote their entire lives to writing songs, listening to music, and learning new tunes? They twist their voices through pointless melodies when nature meant them to sound best when used simply and directly. Their fingers are always tapping out rhythms to whatever music is playing in their heads. Even when they're called to handle serious or sad business, you can hear them humming to themselves. These people aren't relaxing — they're just busy with nonsense.
original_excerpt: Do you call these men idle, who make a business of the comb and looking-glass? what of those who devote their lives to composing, hearing, and learning songs, who twist their voices, intended by Nature to sound best and simplest when used straightforwardly, through all the turns of futile melodies: whose fingers are always beating time to some music on which they are inwardly meditating; who, when invited to serious and even sad business may be heard humming an air to themselves?—such people are not at leisure, but are busy about trifles.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: As for their fancy dinner parties — good God, I can't count these as free time when I see how anxiously they arrange their silverware. They fuss over how their servants' clothes are arranged. They watch with bated breath to see how the cook presents the roasted boar. When the signal comes, slave boys rush around doing their jobs. Birds must be carved into perfect pieces. Poor young servants carefully clean up the spit from drunk guests. Through all this, the hosts are trying to look refined and impressive. Their need to show off follows them everywhere — they can't even eat or drink without putting on a performance.
original_excerpt: As for their banquets, by Hercules, I cannot reckon them among their unoccupied times when I see with what anxious care they set out their plate, how laboriously they arrange the girdles of their waiters' tunics, how breathlessly they watch to see how the cook dishes up the wild boar, with what speed, when the signal is given, the slave-boys run to perform their duties, how skilfully birds are carved into pieces of the right size, how painstakingly wretched youths wipe up the spittings of drunken men. By these means men seek credit for taste and grandeur, and their vices follow them so far into their privacy that they can neither eat nor drink without a view to effect.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: I also wouldn't call those men idle who get carried around in chairs and litters, and who wait for their scheduled exercise time as if they're not allowed to skip it. These are men who need someone else to tell them when to bathe, when to swim, when to eat. They've become so soft and weak that they can't even figure out for themselves whether they're hungry.
original_excerpt: Nor should I count those men idle who have themselves carried hither and thither in sedans and litters, and who look forward to their regular hour for taking this exercise as though they were not allowed to omit it: men who are reminded by some one else when to bathe, when to swim, when to dine: they actually reach such a pitch of languid effeminacy as not to be able to find out for themselves whether they are hungry.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: I once heard one of these pampered rich people—though we shouldn't really call it luxury when someone has forgotten how to be human—being carried from his bath and placed in his chair. He asked, 'Am I sitting down?' Can you believe it? A man who doesn't know if he's sitting—how could he know if he's alive? Or if he can see? Or if he has any free time? I honestly can't tell what's worse: if he really didn't know, or if he was just pretending. These people genuinely lose awareness of many things. But they also act like they're unaware of even more. They enjoy some of these failings because they think it proves how wealthy they are. Apparently, only poor, worthless people need to know what they're doing.
original_excerpt: I have heard one of these luxurious folk—if indeed, we ought to give the name of luxury to unlearning the life and habits of a man—when he was carried in men's arms out of the bath and placed in his chair, say inquiringly, "Am I seated?" Do you suppose that such a man as this, who did not know when he was seated, could know whether he was alive, whether he could see, whether he was at leisure? I can hardly say whether I pity him more if he really did not know or if he pretended not to know this. Such people do really become unconscious of much, but they behave as though they were unconscious of much more: they delight in some failings because they consider them to be proofs of happiness: it seems the part of an utterly low and contemptible man to know what he is doing.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: After hearing all this, do you think playwrights have to stretch their imaginations when they make fun of luxury in their comedies? By God, they leave out more than they make up. In our age — which seems to excel only at inventing new vices — so many unbelievable forms of corruption have appeared that you could actually criticize playwrights for not noticing them all. Can you imagine someone so ruined by luxury that he needs another person to tell him whether he's sitting down or not? This man is definitely not living a life of leisure. You need a different word for him: he's sick, or really he's dead. Only someone who knows he's at leisure is truly at leisure. But this poor creature is only half alive if he needs someone else to tell him what position his body is in. How could such a person possibly have control over his time?
original_excerpt: After this, do you suppose that playwrights draw largely upon their imaginations in their burlesques upon luxury: by Hercules, they omit more than they invent; in this age, inventive in this alone, such a number of incredible vices have been produced, that already you are able to reproach the playwrights with omitting to notice them. To think that there should be any one who had so far lost his senses through luxury as to take some one else's opinion as to whether he was sitting or not? This man certainly is not at leisure: you must bestow a different title on him: he is sick, or rather dead: he only is at leisure who feels that he is at leisure: but this creature is only half alive, if he wants some one to tell him what position his body is in. How can such a man be able to dispose of any time?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12
